title: Advanced MCQ Assessment (Tough Level)
description: 40 tough multiple-choice questions across coding, aptitude, technical fundamentals and DSA. 2 marks each, 80 marks in total, no negative marking. One attempt.

questions.code:

printf("%d %d %d", x++, x++, x);

questions.text: In Python, what is the output?
questions.code:

    L.append(a)
    return L
print(f(1)); print(f(2))

questions.text: What is the time complexity of the following recurrence?
Which statement about Java's String vs StringBuilder is correct in a loop appending 10,000 strings?
options: String concatenation is O(n²) overall due to immutability; StringBuilder is O(n)
StringBuilder is slower because it uses more memory

questions.text: What does this JavaScript snippet log?
In C++, what happens when you call delete twice on the same pointer without setting it to nullptr after the first delete?
options: The second call is silently ignored

questions.text: What is the output?
questions.review: Edited: the original also asked 'why does this happen, and what is the correct way to compare floats?', an open question that can't be auto-marked, so it was dropped.

questions.text: Which of these causes a stack overflow fastest for large n?
options: Tail-recursive factorial with no tail-call optimisation applied by the compiler

questions.text: What is printed?
A function is declared static inside a C file but not in a header. What is the primary effect?
options: Its linkage becomes internal: invisible to other translation units

questions.text: A can do a job in 12 days, B in 15 days, and C alone in 20 days, but C works at half efficiency on even-numbered days. If A, B and C start together, on which day is the job completed?
questions.review: Options written by Zeptrax (none were given). Odd days: 1/12 + 1/15 + 1/20 = 0.2; even days: 1/12 + 1/15 + 1/40 = 0.175. After 5 days 0.95 is done, so the job finishes on day 6.

questions.text: Three pipes A, B and C can fill a tank in 10, 15 and 20 hours respectively. Pipe C fills until the tank is half full, then works as an outlet (drains at the same rate). If all three start together on an empty tank, how long until it is full?
questions.review: Options written by Zeptrax; wording clarified (C fills while below half). First half at 13/60 per hour = 30/13 h; second half at 7/60 per hour = 30/7 h; total 600/91 h ≈ 6.59 h.

questions.text: In a row of 40 people, Rohan is 12th from the left. 5 people join between him and the person on his immediate right, so the row now has 45 people. What are his new positions from the left and from the right?
options: 12th from the left, 34th from the right
17th from the left, 29th from the right
12th from the left, 33rd from the right
13th from the left, 33rd from the right
questions.review: Options written by Zeptrax. People joining on his right don't change his position from the left (12th); from the right: 45 − 12 + 1 = 34th.

questions.text: Six people A–F sit around a circular table. A is opposite D. B is one seat clockwise from A. E sits between B and D. C is not next to D. Where does C sit relative to F?
options: One seat clockwise from F (C is next to A)
questions.review: REPAIRED: the original puzzle had no solution (with B two seats clockwise from A, no seat is next to both B and D) and gave no clue to separate C and F. Seats clockwise from A: A, B, E, D, F, C.

questions.text: A code pattern: ZEBRA → 26-5-2-18-1 (each letter's position in the alphabet). Using the same pattern, decode: 20-15-12-9-7-8-20
questions.review: EDITED: the original said 'reverse alphabet position', but its own example uses normal positions (Z = 26, A = 1), so the example's rule was kept. Options written by Zeptrax.

questions.text: Statements: No scientists are poets. All poets are dreamers. Some dreamers are not realists. Conclusion I: No scientists are dreamers. Conclusion II: Some dreamers are not scientists. Which conclusion follows?
questions.review: Options written by Zeptrax. The poets are dreamers who are not scientists, so II follows; nothing rules out a scientist who is a dreamer, so I does not.

questions.text: A cube is painted red on all faces, then cut into 125 (5×5×5) identical smaller cubes. How many small cubes have exactly 2 painted faces, and how many have none?
questions.review: Options written by Zeptrax. Exactly two faces: 12 edges × (5 − 2) = 36; none: 3³ = 27.

questions.text: Data sufficiency: Is x > y? (I) x² > y²  (II) x and y are both negative.
options: Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone
Both statements together are still not sufficient
questions.review: Options written by Zeptrax. Together: both negative and x² > y² means |x| > |y|, so x < y — the question is answered (no).

questions.text: A clock loses 15 minutes every hour (it shows 45 minutes for each real hour). If it was set correctly at 12:00 noon, what will the faulty clock show when the correct time is 6:00 PM?
questions.review: Options written by Zeptrax; wording clarified, because 'loses 15 minutes every hour' could also mean per hour of the faulty clock (giving 4:48 PM). 6 real hours × 45 min = 4 h 30 min shown.

questions.text: In a knockout tournament of 73 players with a standard bracket (the field is filled up to the next power of two with byes in the first round), how many matches are played in total, and how many players get a first-round bye?
questions.review: Options written by Zeptrax; wording clarified. Every match eliminates one player, so 73 − 1 = 72 matches. Bracket of 128: 128 − 73 = 55 byes.

questions.text: Two transactions T1 and T2 both try to update the same row under Read Committed isolation. Which anomaly is this isolation level still vulnerable to, that Repeatable Read prevents?
A table is in 3NF but not in BCNF. What does that imply?
options: It has a non-trivial functional dependency whose determinant is not a candidate key, but the dependent attribute is prime
questions.review: Option (b) reworded slightly: in the original the clause 'that determinant happens to be a prime attribute' described the wrong side of the dependency; for 3NF-but-not-BCNF it is the dependent (right-hand) attribute that is prime.

questions.text: In a system using the Banker's Algorithm, if the system is in a "safe state", what does that guarantee?
options: No process will ever request more resources
There exists at least one safe sequence in which every process can finish
Deadlock is impossible even with future requests

questions.text: Why does TCP use a 3-way handshake instead of a 2-way handshake to establish a connection?
options: To synchronise sequence numbers in both directions and avoid problems from delayed or duplicate old segments
To reduce the number of packets sent

questions.text: A virtual function draw() is declared in a base class and overridden in a derived class, but the base class destructor is NOT virtual. What happens on delete basePtr; when basePtr points to a derived object?
options: No issue, destructors are always virtual
Only the base class destructor runs, so derived resources leak (undefined behavior)

questions.text: In a hash table using open addressing with linear probing, what causes primary clustering, and how does quadratic probing help?
options: Keys that hash anywhere into an occupied run extend that run; quadratic probing jumps by i² so runs don't merge, but keys with the same home slot still share a probe sequence (secondary clustering)
A poor hash function alone; quadratic probing removes every kind of clustering
Deleted entries leave tombstones; quadratic probing avoids tombstones
Clustering only happens with separate chaining; quadratic probing turns the table into chaining
questions.review: Options written by Zeptrax (the original was an open question).

questions.text: Which of these is true about a B+ tree used for database indexing, compared to a plain B-tree?
options: B+ trees store data only in internal nodes
B+ trees store all records in leaf nodes, which are linked for efficient range queries; internal nodes hold only keys
B-trees are always faster for range queries
B+ trees cannot be used for secondary indexes

questions.text: A process is in the waiting state and its required resource becomes available, but a higher-priority process keeps preempting the CPU before the scheduler ever picks it. This is an example of:
In object-oriented design, what distinguishes composition from aggregation in terms of object lifecycle?
options: In composition the contained object's lifetime is bound to the container; in aggregation it can exist independently

questions.text: Under strict SQL (ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY on), why can't a GROUP BY query select a non-aggregated, non-grouped column, and what does MySQL do when that mode is off?
options: A group can have many values for that column, so the result is ambiguous; with the mode off MySQL silently returns a value from an arbitrary row of the group
It forces a full table scan; with the mode off MySQL adds the column to GROUP BY automatically
Non-grouped columns can't be indexed; with the mode off MySQL returns NULL for them
It is only a style rule; both modes return the first row of each group in insertion order
questions.review: Options written by Zeptrax (the original was an open question).

questions.text: You need the k-th smallest element of an unsorted array of n elements. Which approach has the best WORST-CASE time complexity?
options: Sort then index: O(n log n)
Max-heap of size k: O(n log k)
Min-heap of all n elements: O(n log n)

questions.text: A graph has V vertices and E edges. Which statement about Dijkstra's algorithm with a binary min-heap is TRUE?
options: O((V + E) log V), a meaningful improvement over the array-based O(V²) mainly when the graph is sparse
Works correctly with negative edge weights if there is no negative cycle
Requires the graph to be a DAG

questions.text: In a Red-Black tree with n nodes, what is the maximum height, and why does it guarantee O(log n) operations?
options: 2·log₂(n + 1): every root-to-leaf path has the same number of black nodes and no two reds are adjacent, so the longest path is at most twice the shortest
Exactly log₂ n, because the tree is always perfectly balanced
n/2, but rotations make the average O(log n)
1.44·log₂ n, the same bound as AVL trees
questions.review: Options written by Zeptrax (the original was an open question).

questions.text: Which traversal, combined with the IN-ORDER traversal, is sufficient to uniquely reconstruct a binary tree with distinct keys?
options: Pre-order + in-order is sufficient; post-order + in-order is not
Both pre-order + in-order and post-order + in-order are sufficient
In-order alone is always sufficient for a BST

questions.text: What is the amortized time of push_back on a dynamic array (like std::vector or a Python list) that doubles its capacity when full, and how is the bound proven?
options: O(1) amortized: aggregate/accounting (or potential) analysis shows n pushes cost O(n) in total, because the copies sum to less than 2n
O(log n), because the array is resized log n times
O(n), because a resize copies every element
O(1) worst case, because memory allocation takes constant time
questions.review: Options written by Zeptrax (the original was an open question).

questions.text: In a Directed Acyclic Graph, which algorithm finds the shortest paths from a single source, and why is it asymptotically better than Dijkstra here?
options: Topological sort + one relaxation pass, O(V + E)
BFS, O(V + E), regardless of edge weights

questions.text: A hash map uses separate chaining with n keys in m buckets and a good hash function. What is the expected lookup time, and what load factor typically triggers a resize?
options: O(1 + α) with α = n/m; resize when α exceeds about 0.75 (as in Java's HashMap)
O(log n); resize when α exceeds 2
O(1) regardless of α, so it never needs resizing
questions.review: Options written by Zeptrax (the original was an open question).

questions.text: Which of these problems CANNOT be solved optimally by a greedy approach (greedy fails and DP is needed)?
In Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) string matching, what is the purpose of the failure function (LPS array), and what is the overall time to search a pattern of length m in a text of length n?
options: It stores, for each prefix of the pattern, the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix, so after a mismatch the search continues without re-reading text characters; O(n + m)
It stores hashes of pattern windows for quick comparison; O(nm) in the worst case
It sorts the pattern's characters for binary search; O(n log m)
It marks which text positions to skip, like Boyer-Moore; O(n/m)
questions.review: Options written by Zeptrax (the original was an open question).

questions.text: In a trie storing n words of average length L, what is the time for an exact-match search, and why can it beat a hash set for prefix-heavy workloads such as autocomplete?
options: O(L), independent of n; walking a prefix finds every completion directly and shares work between words with common prefixes, while a hash set can't enumerate by prefix
O(log n), because a trie is a balanced search tree
O(n·L), because every word is compared
O(1), because a trie hashes each character
questions.review: Options written by Zeptrax (the original was an open question).
